stimulus: So, Tell Arvani. For a century the story was that the town died of drought — you'll still find that in older textbooks. But the sediment cores tell a different story: through the settlement's final decades, rainfall stayed right around the region's long-term average. Not a slow drying trend, not wild swings from wet to dry, and not some unusual wet period either — ordinary years, one after another. Which removes the easy answer. Now, the storage jars. Everyone assumed grain — big jars, farming town. But the residue analysis came back unambiguous: the large jars had mostly held olive oil, pressed right at the settlement — we have the crushing basins. Not barley from the surrounding fields, not wine hauled in from elsewhere, and no fish residues at all. This was a town producing oil, probably for exchange. What about Kessara, the neighbor? I bring it up for one reason: the team there has been using micro-stratigraphy and full flotation sampling — methods a generation newer than anything used at Arvani — and I want exactly that toolkit brought to our site. To be clear, that is my only point with Kessara: I am not claiming it fell at the same moment, its tablets don't mention Arvani, and whether it carried on afterward is genuinely unsettled. Finally, the earthquake idea. I think it is half right. The tumbled wall sections do look seismic, and the date fits the abandonment — this was no slow decay, and the damage isn't centuries too early. But a town can rebuild walls; this one had rebuilt them before. Shaking may explain some of the damage. It doesn't, by itself, explain why nobody came back.

stimulus: Let's talk about the Serrat caldera, two thousand four to twelve. Start with the ground itself. The GPS and the radar agreed: the uplift sat squarely over the center of the caldera, and — this is the part that puzzled everyone — it went on climbing, millimeter by millimeter, long after the earthquake swarms had stopped. There was no sign of the ground settling back, no cycle of rise and fall, and the deformation was every bit as broad as the first reports said. Steady, quiet inflation. Then the gases. The chemistry wouldn't let you call it magma alone, and you couldn't pin it all on heated groundwater either — the emissions carried both signatures at once, magmatic and hydrothermal together, which points to a mixed source: magma degassing into an active water system. And these were not the tired gases of an old, cooling body; the ratios were fresh. Now, why did everyone take this so seriously? Because of the eighteen-sixties. The opening phase of that episode looked strikingly like what the instruments were now recording — the same quiet inflation, the same gas rise — and that episode, remember, ended in an eruption. Observers back then read the signs correctly, as it happens, and its deposits were quarried away long ago, useless for mapping anything. The resemblance was the whole alarm. Which brings us to the alert level. I'll be blunt: when it was raised in oh-eight, the instruments were saying nothing new that week. The newspapers, though, were saying plenty. No one could call the move late, and there was no protocol forcing anyone's hand. The pressure was coming from the public, and the committee moved with it.

stimulus: The Verrine Hours. Let's start with what the spectroscopy settled last spring: the blue is lapis, everywhere we looked — the Virgin's robe, yes, but even the little border sprays are lapis. There is no cheaper base layer under it; the lapis goes right down to the parchment, and there is no indigo at all, no azurite anywhere in the book. Now here is my larger point about this workshop, the point I want you to take away: what it used was governed by each patron's purse, not by any rule of the craft. A rich commission, and there is lapis in the margins; a modest one, and the same painters worked wonders with cheap blues. It was never about a house style of materials — and for the record, these compositions match no model book we know, nobody confuses these books with Arden work, and stylistically they kept pace with the newest fashions. It was the money. Which is exactly why I keep returning to the account books: the payments simply stop in the third year, mid-campaign, and that is why the last two gatherings sit unfinished. The accounts never name a single assistant, they don't itemize the pigments, frustratingly, and they won't give you dates precise enough to narrow production — but they do record that break in payment. So: is this Anselm's book? I say yes — but not for the reasons usually given. The faces, if anything, look like assistants' work, and the underdrawing is too varied to be one hand. But the page architecture — the layouts, those border systems — no one else in the region built pages that way, and every page sits comfortably within his working life.

stimulus: Marell Atoll, five years after cyclone Osea. The seedling survey came back this spring, and the pattern is odd: nearly everything new is strung along the debris lines — those windrows of wrack the storm left behind. Hardly any seedlings under the parent trees themselves, but along the wrack lines, dense little rows. And to be clear, there was no shortage of seedlings overall, and they were surviving the dry months just fine. Kanari recruitment hasn't collapsed — it has moved. Why? The imperial pigeons disperse the seed, and the follow-up work told us what changed. It isn't the vine — the feeding branches are clear; the vine never reached them. The rats we could rule out too: the exclosures made no difference. And fruiting still lines up with the breeding season the way it always has. No — the flocks are simply too small now. A crop that three hundred birds once cleared in a week hangs there, drops, and rots before the remaining dozens get to it. The storm surge then rakes the fallen fruit into the wrack lines — hence the pattern. Now, people always ask about the mainland kanari forests. I am not pointing to the mainland to say other animals could take over, nor to argue the problem stops at the shoreline, and I am certainly not proposing it as a source of birds. What I am asking is whether anything we learned in those forests transfers to an atoll at all — I doubt the comparison more each year. And yes, we are acting: a small trial, carrying fruit by hand past the surge zone, is already running on the island's two worst-hit stretches. Pigeon counts are still falling, so nobody is waiting on a rebound; we're not opposed to intervening — quite the opposite — and no one has put a translocation of birds on the table.

stimulus: Today, the Taruic vowel shift — and I want to use it to show how much you can squeeze out of very indirect evidence. Start with the vocabulary Taruic shares with its neighbor, Emel. The direction of borrowing isn't in doubt: Taruic into Emel — the cultural terms all run that way. And Emel's borrowed forms keep the old vowels. So the words crossed over before anything had shifted; the shift comes after the borrowing. Each of these words was borrowed once, and once only — there are no doubled forms. Second, how did it spread? It follows the rivers. Every town on the Ossel trade route shifts early; villages a day's walk from the water shift late or not until much later. There is no single center it radiates from. stimulus: The Adriatic storm-warning service. Begin with the wreck of the Stella Maris in December 1873 — two hundred and eleven lives. I tell that story for one reason: it is the event that put the money on the table. Parliament had debated a warning network for years and done nothing; six weeks after the wreck, the funds were voted. Note the order of events — there was no service yet to blame, and no warning had been issued, because none existed to issue. The service's first decade was, honestly, unimpressive. Its second was much better, and here is why: the agreement of 1885. The Adriatic service and its rival, the Austrian network up the coast, began exchanging observations daily by wire. Seeing the rival's pressure field beside your own — that is what sharpened the warnings. The telegraph itself had linked the stations from the very first season, barometers had been the basis of the warnings from day one, and the scheme to pay fishing crews for reports never got past a proposal. It was the pooling that did it. Those barometer ledgers, by the way, survive nearly complete, gathered in one archive in Trieste, and a recalibration team has recently been through the whole series. Their finding: the readings ran consistently low, about two millibars, instrument after instrument. Climate researchers, so far, have shown no interest in the series. And Marini, the founder? A brilliant promoter — the subscriptions, the lecture tours, the medals — but his claims ran well ahead of what his barometers could show. His statistics, it must be said, were ordinary; the organization, frankly, was held together with string; and the public never lost faith in him, not even at the end.

stimulus: Today, Fantin's dance suites — specifically the set of manuscript parts kept at Welden. Start with their condition, because it surprised everyone. These are not working copies. The corners are crisp, there are no performers' markings, no wax, and what little rubbing exists is uniform from the first suite to the last. Nor can you blame later readers: there are no library stamps, no shelf wear, nothing added after the parts arrived. As far as we can tell, these parts were never played from at all — a set made to be looked at. Now, Casperi. Why does that court matter? One document: a letter written there in seventeen twenty-two, describing Fantin himself leading the suites from the violin — our only eyewitness account. Casperi's payment books never mention the suites, its band was about the same size as Welden's, and the printed dedication names the Duke of Welden, exactly as you would expect. The letter is the prize. Were these pieces for actual dancing? I say yes, and the scores tell you so themselves: the repeat schemes fit the surviving choreographies figure for figure, and that holds for every movement, first to last. The tempo markings are perfectly danceable, and the court ledger tells us nothing either way. Finally, the missing second-violin book. The editors will not invent the line themselves, and they refuse to print the suites with a hole in the texture. The rumored amateur copy has never been traced. So those suites wait — set aside for the final volume, once everything else is out.
